Updated assessment incorporating the August 2017 Beige Book and July 2017 SLOOS:
- Macro backdrop: The Beige Book (published in September, covering conditions through late August) reported modest-to-moderate growth across most Districts with continued labor-market tightness. However, Hurricanes Harvey (with Irma and Maria shortly thereafter) caused notable near-term disruptions concentrated along the Gulf Coast—particularly in the energy and natural resources sector (including the Eagle Ford), with shutdowns in oil and natural gas production—and affected the Dallas and Atlanta Districts. Agricultural conditions were mixed. These impacts align with the FOMC’s view that storms will temporarily affect activity and lift gasoline prices but are unlikely to alter the medium-term national outlook.
- Credit conditions: SLOOS continues to signal soft spots—domestic banks saw weaker demand for CRE and consumer credit (auto and credit cards) and tighter standards in those consumer categories; foreign banks tightened C&I and CRE standards even as they reported stronger CRE demand. Mortgage credit eased (jumbo, QM, GSE-conforming), offering some support to housing.
- Policy context: Consistent with an economy expanding at a moderate pace with inflation below 2% in the near term, the FOMC held the funds rate at 1 to 1-1/4 percent and will begin balance sheet normalization in October.
- Implication: Overall conditions remain positive and financial conditions accommodative, but the Beige Book’s hurricane-related disruptions and the SLOOS’s selective tightening/soft demand modestly temper the near-term outlook. Temporary inflation firming from gasoline is likely, but the broader inflation picture remains subdued.

Net: Still positive, but a bit less upbeat after factoring in hurricane disruptions and softer credit demand; partially offset by easier mortgage credit and ongoing labor-market strength.
